recall.minute: Tables cannot store or generalise over the vast state spaces of real problems (Pacman, images, continuous positions), so we approximate v̂(s, w) ≈ v_π(s) with far fewer weights than states, commonly linear v̂ = wᵀx(s). We minimise the on-policy-weighted value error by SGD, w ← w + α[Uₜ − v̂]∇v̂ with ∇v̂ = x(s) for linear functions. Gradient MC uses Uₜ = Gₜ (true gradient, converges to a VE minimum); semi-gradient TD uses R + γv̂(S′, w), ignoring the target's dependence on w; it learns faster and converges to the TD fixed point for linear on-policy learning. Worked: x(s) = [1, 2], x(s′) = [0, 1], w = [0.5, 0.1], r = 1, γ = 0.9, α = 0.1 gives δ = 0.39 and w = [0.539, 0.178]. Features: state aggregation, coarse coding, tile coding (offset grids, one tile active per tiling), RBFs; neural networks learn features and generalise globally. Combining approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy training (the deadly triad) can diverge, as in Baird's counterexample.
